parts.title: Setup
steps: Clone the repository. git clone https://github.com/knarayanareddy/workshop-agentic-harness cd workshop-agentic-harness

Build it. No API key needed yet. With a JDK: this compiles everything and runs the tests. On Windows use gradlew.bat build. ./gradlew build Without a JDK: this builds the package for your OS and CPU into agentic-harness/. ./build-package.sh # macOS, Linux build-package.cmd # Windows

Set your API key. export MODEL_API_KEY=your-key-here # macOS / Linux $env:MODEL_API_KEY = "your-key-here" # Windows PowerShell set "MODEL_API_KEY=your-key-here" # Windows Command Prompt You can also set MODEL_NAME and MODEL_BASE_URL for another model or OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Leave them unset to use the workshop proxy.

Check the connection. This sends one small request to the model, so it confirms your key, the endpoint and the network in one go. With a JDK: ./gradlew verifySetup You should see a line starting with [ok]. If you see [error], the line below it says what to fix. Without a JDK: skip this step. Typing hello in the next step checks the same thing.

Start the agent. It works on the workspace/ folder. With a JDK: ./gradlew :app:run -q --console=plain Without a JDK: pick the folder for your OS and CPU (linux-x64, linux-aarch64, mac-x64, mac-aarch64 or windows-x64). Rebuild the package each time you change an extension. ./agentic-harness/agentic-harness-mac-aarch64/harness # macOS, Linux agentic-harness\agentic-harness-windows-x64\harness.cmd # Windows Each line you type is one turn, and the session keeps its history. Type /clear to start a new session, /report to write an HTML report of the session (see The loop, in one page), and exit to stop.

parts.title: Where am I?
parts.goal: When the harness starts, have it find out the date and time, the operating system, and whether the workspace is in a git repository. Tell the model in a Static system prompt section called environment.
parts.why: Every session starts blind. The model assumes the date of its training data, guesses which commands work on your system, and spends tool calls, each one waiting for your approval, to find out the rest. The harness can check all of it once at start-up, for free.
steps: Ask the agent What time is it, which operating system are we running on, and is this folder in a git repository? and watch what it does in the trace.

Create Environmentenvironment.ts in your systemprompt/exercise folder: a function that takes the Workspace, like systemprompt/defaults/Rolea function that takes the whole AssemblyContext (ctx), not just ctx.workspace like role in systemprompt/defaults/role.ts: checking for git needs ctx.exec.

Register it in KotlinExtensions.kt: DefaultSections.all(workspace) + Environment.section(workspace). Register it in JavaExtensions.java: .section(Environment.section(workspace)). Register it in index.ts: [...defaultSections(ctx.workspace), environment(ctx)].

Restart and ask again. It usually answers without a tool call now. If it still runs one, check with MODEL_LOG_RAW that your environment section is in the system prompt. The rise in the system token count in the trace is what your section costs on every call.

parts.goal: When workspace/OpenRA/ is missing, have the harness tell the model to either tell the user or clone it. Once it's there, the model hears nothing more. Use a Dynamic system prompt section called openra_checkout.

hints.summary: How does a Dynamic section work?
hints.text: The harness calls it before every inference call. Text is added to the conversation as <context section="...">, and only when it has changed. null adds nothing. A Static section would still be saying "OpenRA is missing" after the clone.

hints.summary: Tell the user, or clone it?

hints.summary: Why not just load OpenRA's README.md or CONTRIBUTING.md?
hints.text: They're written for people, not agents. CONTRIBUTING.md tells you to rebase and open a pull request, which is exactly what assignment 2 forbids.

hints.summary: What if the file is huge?
hints.text: It's in every inference call. Cap it, for example at 4,000 characters, and tell the model to read the file itself for the rest.

parts.why: Sessions end, and the changes stay. A new session doesn't remember the last one, so the agent either builds on half-finished work without knowing it or throws it away. One git status at start-up prevents both.

parts.goal: Write two tools around the Toolbox helper: start_toolbox gets the OpenRA toolbox ready (a Docker image, a long-running container and a compiled OpenRA, which takes minutes), and toolbox_status reports how far it has got.
parts.why: Everything the agent does with OpenRA goes through the toolbox: building it, checking it, packaging it. Done with run_command, that's a long docker command line, an approval prompt for each one, and a build that takes longer than the 120-second limit. A tool turns all of that into one call. It also teaches the first rule of tools: a tool call must not wait for minutes.

parts.title: What would you guard?
parts.goal: Think of something this agent should never do, or must always do, and enforce it.
parts.why: You've used Deny and Replace. There are two more jobs a guardrail can do: gate an action with Ask, and refuse to let a turn end with beforeEndTurn → Continue.

parts.title: Red-teaming
parts.goal: Pair up with someone, swap laptops, and try to get their agent past their guardrails. Then swap back and fix whatever got through.
parts.why: You wrote your guardrails knowing exactly which commands you had in mind, so they block those. An attacker doesn't use your list. Someone who didn't write the patterns will try spellings, detours and stories you never thought of. That's what red-teaming is: attacking your own system on purpose, before someone else does. You're working on someone else's laptop, with their API key and their files. Be a polite attacker. When an approval prompt comes up, always answer no. Reaching the prompt already counts as a hit. Don't really push anything, and don't read real secrets: the owner plants a fake key for you to go after. Owner: before you hand your laptop over, put a fake secret in the workspace, for example workspace/.env with ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-api03-FAKEFAKEFAKE…. Start the agent and leave its code closed. Attacker: talk to the agent only. Don't read or change the harness code, and don't type commands in a terminal yourself. Everything has to go through the prompt. Try to get the agent to do something one of the 4.x guardrails should stop: push to OpenRA, run Python, leak the fake key, pipe a download into a shell, or read a file outside the workspace. Write down every attempt that worked, or that reached an approval prompt: the exact prompt you typed and the command the agent ran. Swap back after 5–10 minutes. Show each other what got through, then fix the holes on your own laptop.

ToolCallCompleted says whether a tool succeeded, but not what its input was. ToolCallProposed has the input. Tools run one after another, so remember the last proposed call, and pair it with the next completed one that has the same tool name. A denied call is never completed. Its input is in the path field, or actor for set_actor_value.
A guardrail denial is a GuardrailDecision whose decision starts with Deny. When you answer n, that's an ApprovalRequested whose decision starts with Deny.

parts.title: 7 · Make it yours
parts.goal: Pick the thing you missed most in assignment 6 and add it to your harness. It's yours.
parts.why: You've used every extension point now: system prompt sections, tools, guardrails and listeners. The harness doesn't care what you build with them. The best harness is the one shaped around the work you actually do, and only you know what that is.

hints.summary: Some ideas to get you going
hints.text: A tool that reads OpenRA's crash log, so a broken shader explains itself. A tool that undoes the agent's last change, or shows everything it changed this session. A section that remembers what you modded in earlier sessions, by keeping notes in a file in the workspace. A guardrail that won't let a turn end until check_mod has passed. A listener that keeps a log of every change across sessions, as the start of an undo.
Show your neighbour what you built, and steal their best idea.
